analysis.one_liner: Makes federal wage, safety, anti-discrimination, and family leave laws apply to congressional employees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 1994 with no cosponsors, sent to five House committees, and never received a committee or floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Congress was already exempt from most federal workplace laws that cover everyone else. This bill would have applied ten of them — covering minimum wage and overtime, race and sex discrimination, disability and age discrimination, workplace safety, family and medical leave, union rights, and advance notice of layoffs — to House and Senate employees. It also created an Office of Compliance to enforce those rights through counseling, mediation, hearings, and court access.
analysis.who_benefits: House, Senate, and Architect of the Capitol employees — the aides, clerks, and staff who work in Congress — would gain the same protections against underpayment, discrimination, unsafe conditions, and arbitrary firing that workers elsewhere already have.

how_it_helps.text: Applies ten federal employment laws — including the Fair Labor Standards Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, and the Family and Medical Leave Act — to the legislative branch, most taking effect within a year of enactment.

Creates an Office of Compliance that runs a step-by-step process for employees: confidential counseling, mediation, a hearing before three independent officers, and a court route as an alternative, with attorney's fees available to employees who prevail.
Makes it an unlawful employment practice for a Member, Senator, or their offices to intimidate or retaliate against an employee for using these rights.
Requires the Office to educate employees about their rights and to compile statistics and demographic data on the congressional workforce, including race, sex, and wages.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and other congressional employing offices would bear the cost of complying — paying overtime, fixing unsafe conditions, changing discriminatory practices — and compensation awards would come from House and Senate funds rather than from Members personally.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their offices

drawbacks.text: The process is largely confidential: counseling, mediation, and hearings are all sealed, which means employees who settle or lose a claim cannot warn others about an office with a pattern of mistreatment.
Members and heads of employing offices are shielded from personal liability for compensation awards, and the hearing board cannot award punitive damages.

The bill lets employers consider party affiliation, domicile, and 'political compatibility' in employment decisions, and it makes the process the exclusive route to court, cutting off ordinary lawsuits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — ending Congress's exemption from basic workplace law — is straightforwardly fair and would have real value for the roughly thousands of people on congressional payrolls. The trade-offs are real but secondary: the confidentiality rules and the ban on punitive damages and personal liability would have made the system friendlier to employers than the regular courts are. A flawed version of accountability is still substantially better than none.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final months of the session with no cosponsors, split among five House committees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Moakley introduced the Congressional Accountability Act on August 3, 1994.
The bill was referred to five House committees at once — House Administration, Education and Labor, Government Operations, Rules, and Judiciary — which means any committee could have blocked it.
Over the following six weeks it was referred to several subcommittees, and action notices pointed to the related bill H.R. 4822.
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred; the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their offices were better off: by letting the bill die, they kept their exemption from the wage, safety, and anti-discrimination laws that applied to every other employer for the rest of the session.

for.name: Rep. Joe Moakley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to five House committees.

against.name: Leaders of the five House committees of referral
against.role: Education and Labor, Government Operations, House Administration, Rules, and Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measured partisan split.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and congressional employing offices
industries.note: Passage would have made House and Senate offices subject to the same wage, safety, and anti-discrimination law as other employers, ending a long-standing exemption. Their interest in keeping that exemption ran directly against the staff the law would have protected.
